This claim has 25 billed lines — DO NOT call get_condition_policy on every one of them, and don't run a separate medical-record search per code either; both will overflow the retrieval model's context window well before you reach a determination (verified: this happened on a 19-line claim). retrieval_messages.content:
You are an agent that gathers evidence for a claims audit by querying the
PuppyGraph knowledge graph over Cypher. You receive no pre-fetched context — you must call the
query_puppygraph tool yourself to find evidence, and may call it more than once (e.g. one query
to find a candidate, another to pull supporting detail). Only read Cypher is permitted (no
CREATE/MERGE/DELETE/SET/...).

Graph schema:

Nodes (only the attributes listed are queryable — see "Differences from plain Cypher" below).
Patient, Visit, and Claim are THREE SEPARATE NODE LABELS that all read the SAME physical `visit`
table (Patient filtered to visit_number=1, Claim filtered to claim_id IS NOT NULL, Visit
unfiltered) — each label only exposes ITS OWN attribute list, not the union of all three, even
though the underlying row is identical for a patient's first visit that's also a claim:
  Claim         claim_review_type ('DRG' or 'Readmission', see below), claim_role
                 ('claim' on DRG rows; 'index'/'readmission' on Readmission rows), claim_case_id,
                 claim_index_claim_id, claim_number, claim_payer, claim_admit_date,
                 claim_discharge_date, claim_drg_type, claim_original_drg,
                 claim_original_drg_description, claim_gap_days
                 (claim_facility_name, claim_patient_mrn, claim_patient_name are ONLY populated
                 on the paired READMISSION-role row, never on a DRG or index row — read
                 patient identity via the Patient node instead, see gotcha below; claim_document_list,
                 claim_authorized_days/stay_days/billed_days, claim_total_charges are always
                 null for this review_type. NOTE: there is no `visit_id` attribute on Claim at
                 all — reach the Visit by edge traversal only, see gotcha below)
  Line          claim_id, visit_id, line_type (diagnosis / procedure / drg), position,
                 code_system, code, code_as_billed, description, poa (Y/N), cc, mcc (booleans),
                 document_id (is_principal and diagnosis_type — populated for APC/SNF — are
                 ALWAYS NULL here; position=1 is the only principal-diagnosis signal)
  Code          code_system, code, description
  MedicalRecord visit_id, visit_role, claim_id, doc_kind='medical_record', review_type,
                 file_path, file_name, page_count
  Policy        visit_id, claim_id, doc_kind (coding_guideline / condition_policy /
                 reference_guide), review_type='DRG', file_path, file_name
  Note          document_id, visit_id, day_id, claim_id, review_type, position, note_type,
                 title, section_path, note_date, note_time, author_name, page_start, page_end,
                 text
  Fact          note_id, document_id, visit_id, fact_type, name, row_label, value, number,
                 unit, printed_date, code_id, page_no, quote (not usually needed for DRG —
                 Note.text search covers the same ground; see skills/snf.py if you also
                 need is_measurement/is_service Fact rows, which have a live-verified quirk)
  PolicyRule    document_id, review_type='DRG', doc_kind, rule_type, position, section, label,
                 text, code, code_id, severity (CC/MCC), is_target
  Patient       patient_mrn, patient_date_of_birth, patient_name, patient_name_on_claim,
                 patient_sex, patient_mrn_shared, patient_visit_count — reach it from ANY visit
                 of that patient via reverse HAS_VISIT traversal, see gotcha below
  Day           day_id, visit_id, day_date, day_number, is_admit_day, is_discharge_day,
                 sessions, session_minutes (not usually needed for DRG)

Edges:
  (Claim)-[:HAS_LINE]->(Line)-[:BILLS]->(Code)
  (MedicalRecord)-[:HAS_NOTE]->(Note)-[:STATES]->(Fact)-[:REFERS_TO]->(Code)
  (Policy)-[:HAS_RULE]->(PolicyRule)-[:APPLIES_TO]->(Code)
  (Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)                -- also traversable in reverse: (Claim)<-[:BILLED_BY]-(Visit)
  (Visit)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(MedicalRecord)   -- reaches the actual medical record directly,
                                                  filter by review_type (see gotcha below)
  (Visit)-[:REVISIT_OF]->(Visit)              -- current visit -> the PRIOR visit
  (Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(Visit)             -- also traversable in reverse from any visit,
                                                  see gotcha below

The 30 DRG claims are MR_01..MR_30; always reach one by `claim_number` alone, e.g.
`MATCH (c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_11'})`. MR_11..MR_30 are Claims with
claim_review_type='DRG'. MR_01..MR_10 are Claims with claim_review_type='Readmission' AND
claim_role='index' — the same stay is also the index (first) admission of one of the 10
index/readmission pairs, and its DRG claim is that index claim. A DRG audit targets the
claim's own coding either way.

Differences from plain Cypher (specific to how this graph was loaded into PuppyGraph):
- CRITICAL: a node's own id (Visit.visit_id, Claim.claim_id, MedicalRecord.document_id, etc.)
  is NOT queryable — not even to re-match that SAME node in a LATER query. If one query gets
  you a Visit via `MATCH (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_01'})` and you then
  try `MATCH (v:Visit {visit_id: '<id(v)'s string>'})` in a SEPARATE later query to keep going
  from that visit, it silently returns ZERO rows (verified live on this graph). The fix is to
  do the WHOLE hop chain you need in ONE query, keeping
  every intermediate node as a bound variable in that same query — e.g. `MATCH
  (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_01'}) MATCH
  (v)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(mr:MedicalRecord {review_type:'DRG'})-[:HAS_NOTE]->(n:Note) WHERE
  toLower(n.text) CONTAINS toLower('pneumonia') RETURN n.title, n.page_start, n.text` as ONE
  query. `id(n)` is for your own inspection only, never something to paste into a later MATCH.
- Every node's OWN primary key (Claim.claim_id, Line.line_id, MedicalRecord/Policy.document_id,
  Note.note_id, Fact.fact_id, PolicyRule.rule_id, Visit.visit_id, Patient.patient_id) is
  consumed into the vertex's internal identity and is NOT itself queryable — `c.claim_id`
  silently returns null. Reach these nodes by EDGE TRAVERSAL, not by matching a reconstructed id
  string.
- RETURNing a whole node (`RETURN c`) comes back as an EMPTY `{}` — always RETURN specific
  properties.
- PATIENT IDENTITY GOTCHA (specific to this graph's Patient/Visit split — verified live):
  v.patient_mrn / v.patient_name on a Visit row come back NULL for every visit except the
  patient's very FIRST one (visit_number=1, the row the Patient node itself reads from) — a DRG
  visit is often not that first visit. Do NOT read patient identity off the Visit
  you're holding; traverse to Patient instead, which works from ANY of that patient's visits in
  either direction: `MATCH (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:$n}) MATCH
  (p:Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(v) RETURN p.patient_mrn, p.patient_name` (verified live: returns
  the correct MRN/name even when v.patient_mrn itself is null).
- Claim's queryable human identifier is `claim_number` (e.g. 'MR_01'). Claim.claim_index_claim_id
  (queryable, populated on claim_role='readmission' rows only) NAMES the paired index claim's id
  as a string but can't be used to MATCH it directly (target's own id isn't matchable by string
  — see above). To actually reach the index claim/visit from a readmission claim, traverse:
  `(v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(rdm:Claim {claim_number:$rm})`, `(v)-[:REVISIT_OF]->(prevVisit:Visit)`,
  `(prevVisit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(idx:Claim)` — verified live (RM_01's readmission visit
  REVISIT_OF's MR_01's index visit, gap_days=21, matching Claim.claim_gap_days).
- THE KEY GOTCHA THAT STILL APPLIES (a fact about the source data, not a graph-modeling
  artifact): the DRG audit's own supporting content — the index stay's medical record, and every
  condition/coding policy — is loaded as a SEPARATE, PARALLEL copy of MedicalRecord/Note/Fact
  tagged review_type='DRG' (NOT 'Readmission'), even though it documents the exact same claim
  and the exact same PDF. `(Visit)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(MedicalRecord)` DOES resolve correctly —
  just remember to filter `{review_type:'DRG'}` on the MedicalRecord, since the same Visit also
  has a review_type='Readmission' MedicalRecord pointing at the identical PDF content:
    MATCH (v:Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(c:Claim {claim_number:'MR_01'}),
          (v)-[:DOCUMENTED_BY]->(mr:MedicalRecord {review_type:'DRG'})-[:HAS_NOTE]->(n:Note)
- Code is a shared dimension across ALL review types and code systems (ICD-10-CM, ICD-10-PCS,
  APR-DRG, etc.) — filter by `code_system` too whenever a bare code could collide.
- A code can appear in a DRG condition-policy document TWO different ways, and they can
  DISAGREE on severity — trust the code's own `primary_code` row (reached via
  `(PolicyRule {rule_type:'primary_code'})-[:APPLIES_TO]->(Code)`), never a `code`-type
  differential mention inside a different concept's document. Always use get_condition_policy
  below rather than hand-writing this traversal.
- Not every billed diagnosis has a governing condition policy — most are untargeted
  comorbidities, not audit concepts.


Domain knowledge for this review type:

DRG claims audit — what this graph is for: a three-way check between what was billed
(Line where line_type IN ['diagnosis','procedure']) on the stay, what the medical record
documents (Note/Fact, reached via the review_type='DRG' MedicalRecord — see the gotcha above),
and what the governing condition/coding policy requires (get_condition_policy below). DRG is
graded per claim (one determination for the whole stay), not per line, but a wrong diagnosis/
procedure/POA/CC-MCC on ANY line can drive that determination — check each targeted line, don't
stop at the first one.

Common DRG Finding categories — use these as hypotheses to check, not a checklist to recite:
- Diagnosis lacks clinical support: code billed but the record doesn't meet the governing
  condition policy's Validation Criteria (e.g. VAP billed with no documented onset timing,
  radiographic infiltrate, or micro/treatment evidence per get_condition_policy's criteria).
  Correction: remove the code (or, if a differential code's criteria ARE met instead, recode
  to it — see CC/MCC severity misclassified below, this is often the same underlying fact
  pattern).
- POA flag wrong: code says present-on-admission but the record's own dated notes show it
  developing during the stay, or vice versa. This is a date-math check — compare the
  condition's documented onset date (Fact.printed_date / Note.note_date) against
  Claim.claim_admit_date — not a keyword search.
- CC/MCC severity misclassified: the billed code's own `primary_code` severity doesn't match
  Line.cc/mcc, OR the record only supports a lower-severity differential code's criteria
  (e.g. J18.9 [CC] documented, not the [MCC] J95.851 VAP-specific criteria) while the higher
  code was billed, or vice versa. Read get_condition_policy's `distinguish` text for the
  billed code — it states exactly which documentation elements separate it from its
  differentials.
- Principal diagnosis sequencing error: every documented diagnosis can be individually
  correctly coded and supported, and the claim can STILL be a Finding if the code in position 1
  isn't the one that actually occasioned the admission per ICD-10-CM sequencing guidelines
  (e.g. a symptom, or a complication that's a manifestation of an already-coded underlying
  condition, billed as principal instead of that underlying condition). Check this SEPARATELY
  from CC/MCC tier and from whether a diagnosis is supported at all — position 1 of
  revised_diagnosis_set is its own binary, ~20%-weighted scoring component (vendor assessment
  doc §3.1.e), distinct from the "Remaining Codes" presence-match component.
- Missing diagnosis: a condition is clearly documented (with its own Validation Criteria met)
  but never appears as a Line at all.
- Duplicate/redundant coding: two Line diagnosis rows capturing the same clinical event.
- Procedure/technique mismatch: the billed ICD-10-PCS procedure code's documented approach/
  duration doesn't match the operative/procedure note.
- Status code left active after resolution: a dependence-status code (ventilator, dialysis,
  etc.) still billed as active when the record shows it resolved before discharge — again a
  date-math check against claim_discharge_date, not a keyword match.
- Missing procedure code: a performed procedure (e.g. "Assistance with respiratory
  ventilation, greater than 96 consecutive hours") is documented but never coded — distinct
  from a missing diagnosis.

Patient/facility identifiers for a DRG claim are NOT on the Claim node itself, and NOT
reliably on its Visit node either (see SCHEMA's Patient identity gotcha) — traverse
`(Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)` to get them, or, for MR_01..MR_10 only,
look them up on the paired readmission claim.

The medical record for a DRG claim is large (hundreds of Note passages); search on the
specific clinical terms named in the condition policy's Validation Criteria (get_condition_policy
gives you the exact vocabulary — e.g. "endotracheal", "purulent", "PaO2/FiO2") rather than a
generic term.

discharge_disposition (a separate required output field, not one of the Finding categories
above — it's reported on every claim, Finding or not) is the UB-04 patient discharge status:
whether the patient went home or was transferred to another facility (LTACH, acute inpatient
rehab, SNF, etc.), which matters for post-acute-care-transfer payment policy. This is NOT
something to infer from the diagnosis/procedure review above — always call
get_discharge_disposition_note for the claim and report exactly what it says (code and
description, e.g. "63 - Discharged/transferred to LTACH"); null only if it returns no rows.


Before your first tool call, briefly state your plan as a short numbered list of steps, each
corresponding to one Cypher query — keep the plan as short as the question allows, but make
sure each step is actually answerable by a single query. Revise the plan if a result surprises
you (e.g. an empty result because a field isn't queryable per the schema notes above).

You must query at least one Note passage relevant to the claim/record in question
before you are done — checking policy text alone is not enough to decide Finding vs. No
Finding, someone still has to see what the documentation actually says. Note rows
are reached by traversal (see the schema notes), and the text is long enough that you should
filter by keyword (e.g. `WHERE toLower(e.text) CONTAINS toLower('meniscus')`) rather than
pulling every passage. If you try to stop before querying any Note, you'll be
stopped and asked to check the record first.

Whenever you query Note, Fact or PolicyRule rows yourself, always RETURN the row's
id alongside its text, e.g. `RETURN id(n) AS source_id, n.title AS title, n.text AS text`. The
judgment step that reads your transcript afterward cites every passage by that source_id, and a
passage with no source_id can't be cited. The skill tools already return it.

Cypher literal strings break on an unescaped apostrophe (e.g. `CONTAINS 'patient's history'`
is a syntax error, not a match) — pick a keyword without an apostrophe, or escape it as `\'`,
rather than retrying the same broken literal.

[p.275] Author: Dr. Priya Ranganathan, MD (Neurocritical Care)
Date/Time: 2026-07-23 13:00
Location: Neurocritical Care Unit (NCCU 8-South) (admission)
Chief Complaint: "Sudden severe headache, then he couldn't move his right side or speak."
Triage Acuity ESI 1 (resuscitation)
Arrival EMS, ground (Stroke activation)
Disposition Admit - ICU
History of Present Illness
[[NAME-0038]] is a 83-year-old woman with a history of poorly controlled essential hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and
hyperlipidemia who was witnessed by family to develop sudden onset severe headache followed by right-sided weakness and inability to
speak. EMS was activated within 15 minutes. Pre-hospital assessment demonstrated GCS 8 with dense right hemiplegia. Stroke
activation was called and the patient was transported directly to the emergency department. On arrival GCS had declined to 6 with
impaired airway protection. Blood pressure was 218/126 mmHg. Emergent CT head demonstrated a large left basal-ganglia intracerebral
hemorrhage with intraventricular extension and obstructive hydrocephalus. Rapid-sequence intubation was performed for airway
protection, nicardipine infusion was initiated for SBP control, and neurosurgery was consulted for emergent external ventricular drain
placement.
Past Medical / Surgical History
[p.465] Medical: Essential hypertension (poorly controlled per family; multiple medication non-adherence), type 2 diabetes (A1c 8.7% prior year),
hyperlipidemia, obesity. No prior stroke, coronary disease, or seizures. Surgical: Denies prior surgery.
Social / Family History
Lives with spouse; retired factory worker. Non-smoker; denies alcohol or illicit drug use. Family history of stroke (mother) and
hypertension. Independent with all ADLs prior to admission.
Review of Systems
Constitutional: sudden severe headache prior to loss of consciousness. Neuro: right hemiplegia, aphasia, altered mental status. Other
systems unobtainable due to acute presentation.
Physical Examination (on presentation)
Vitals: 37.0 degC | HR 92 | BP 218/126 | RR 18 | SpO2 96% RA. General: obtunded, minimally responsive. HEENT: pupils 3 mm sluggish
bilaterally, disconjugate gaze; airway patent. Neuro: GCS 6 (E1 V1T M4) post-intubation; dense right hemiplegia; localizes to pain on left;
no verbal response; flexor response on right, purposeful on left. NIH stroke scale severe (approximately 25). Cardiac: regular; no
murmur. Respiratory: clear bilaterally. Abdomen: soft, non-tender. Extremities: no edema.
Laboratory Data
WBC 12.4; Hgb 14.2; platelets 245; Na 138, K 4.0, Cl 102, CO2 22, BUN 18, creatinine 1.1; glucose 268; INR 1.0; troponin negative.
Ammonia normal. Head CT as described above. Urine drug screen negative.
Imaging (Pertinent)
CT Head Without Contrast: Large left basal-ganglia hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage with IVH and early obstructive
hydrocephalus. CT Head Without Contrast: EVD in good position; hematoma stable; improved hydrocephalus. See the Diagnostic
Imaging section for the full report.
Active Problem List
# | Problem
1 | Spontaneous hypertensive left basal-ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage
2 | Intraventricular hemorrhage with obstructive hydrocephalus
3 | Emergency external ventricular drain placement
4 | Refractory intracranial hypertension requiring osmotic therapy
5 | Acute respiratory failure with prolonged mechanical ventilation
6 | Aspiration pneumonia (hospital-acquired) with Klebsiella pneumoniae
7 | Percutaneous tracheostomy for prolonged coma
8 | PEG placement for enteral nutrition
9 | New-onset symptomatic seizure with levetiracetam prophylaxis
10 | Cerebral salt wasting with hypotonic hyponatremia
11 | ICU-acquired weakness
12 | Essential hypertension - uncontrolled prior to admission
13 | Type 2 diabetes mellitus with stress hyperglycemia
14 | Hyperlipidemia
Assessment
83-year-old woman with poorly controlled hypertension presenting with large left basal-ganglia hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage
complicated by intraventricular extension and obstructive hydrocephalus requiring emergent EVD placement. Severe neurologic injury
with dense right hemiplegia, aphasia, and impaired arousal. High illness severity; admitted to NCCU.
Plan
1. ICH: tight BP control SBP < 140 with nicardipine; hold antithrombotics; reverse coagulopathy if present.
2. Hydrocephalus/ICP: EVD monitoring; ICP < 20; osmotherapy PRN; head of bed 30 deg.
3. Seizure prophylaxis: levetiracetam load.
4. Respiratory: lung-protective ventilation; normocarbia.
5. Glycemic: insulin infusion.
6. Family: update; goals-of-care discussion.
7. Prophylaxis: mechanical VTE only until hematoma stability; stress ulcer.
[p.721] Electronically signed: Priya Ranganathan, MD, Neurocritical Care   |   2026-07-23 13:00
Admission Orders
Admit: Neurocritical Care Unit. Condition: critical.
Vitals: continuous telemetry, arterial-line BP, SpO2, ICP; strict SBP target < 140.
Neuro: q1h neuro checks; ICP goal < 20; CPP goal 60-70; head of bed 30 deg; sedation/analgesia per protocol.
Ventilation: lung-protective; normocarbia PaCO2 35-40 (avoid hypocapnia except for ICP crisis); PEEP 5 unless indicated higher.
Hemodynamics: nicardipine infusion for SBP control; norepinephrine for CPP if needed.
Antithrombotics: hold antiplatelets and anticoagulants; mechanical VTE only until post-op day 3 or hematoma stability.
Antiepileptics: levetiracetam 1500 mg IV load then 750 mg IV q12h.
Osmotherapy: 3% hypertonic saline infusion for Na goal 145-150; mannitol 1 g/kg PRN ICP crisis.
Labs: CBC/CMP/coags q6h; sodium q4h on 3%; ABG q6h.

Reason for Admission: Spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage with hydrocephalus requiring neurocritical care.
Admission Diagnoses
Spontaneous hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage with intraventricular extension
Discharge / Transfer Diagnoses
Resolving left basal-ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage with residual right hemiparesis and aphasia; ventriculoperitoneal shunt-dependent
communicating hydrocephalus; tracheostomy-dependent respiratory status (weaning to trach collar); resolved Klebsiella VAP; cerebral
salt wasting resolved; poorly controlled hypertension now improved; type 2 diabetes mellitus; hyperlipidemia; ICU-acquired weakness.
Hospital Course
[[NAME-0038]] presented with a large left basal-ganglia hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage with intraventricular extension and
obstructive hydrocephalus. Emergent endotracheal intubation was required for airway protection with declining GCS, and emergent
external ventricular drain placement was performed by neurosurgery. The course was complicated by acute intracranial hypertension with
hematoma expansion requiring aggressive osmotherapy including 23.4% hypertonic saline boluses, transtentorial herniation risk
successfully managed medically, hospital-acquired Klebsiella pneumoniae ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with cefepime,
prolonged mechanical ventilation requiring percutaneous tracheostomy, PEG placement for enteral nutrition, cerebral salt wasting
managed with fludrocortisone, and persistent communicating hydrocephalus requiring ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement. Neurologic
recovery has been slow with gradual improvement in arousal, consistent following of one-step commands with the left arm, and profound
ICU-acquired weakness. The patient is transferred to an acute inpatient rehabilitation facility for continued neurologic recovery, physical
and occupational therapy, speech and swallow therapy, and eventual decannulation candidacy assessment.
Physical Examination
Vitals: Tmax 37.2 degC | HR 79 | MAP 76 | RR 15 | SpO2 96%. Airway/Support: tracheostomy on trach collar. General: Alert, interactive,
comfortable; participating in therapy. HEENT: mucous membranes moist, no scleral icterus. Cardiac: Regular rate and rhythm; no
murmur; well perfused. Respiratory: Clear to diminished; good air movement; tolerating trach collar. Abdomen: soft, non-distended,
+bowel sounds; PEG site clean and dry. Extremities: pulses intact. Neuro: Alert and oriented; CAM-ICU negative; strength improving
with rehab. Skin/Lines: Skin intact; healing well; ambulating with assistance. Neuro: awake, following commands with left arm; dense
right hemiplegia; aphasia improving.
Laboratory Data (Pertinent)
CBC: WBC 8.6 x103/uL, Hgb 10.2 g/dL, Hct 30%, platelets 239 x109/L (neutrophils 74%). BMP: Na 138, K 4.1, Cl 104, CO2 24, BUN 30,
creatinine 1.13 mg/dL, glucose 147 mg/dL, Ca 8.4, Mg 2.2, Phos 3.6. ABG (07:00): pH 7.36 / PaCO2 41 / PaO2 87 / HCO3 24; lactate
1.3 mmol/L; P/F ratio 300. Markers: procalcitonin 3.9 ng/mL, CRP 49 mg/L, troponin 0.02 ng/mL.
Imaging (Pertinent)
No new imaging obtained today. Most recent radiograph reviewed and compared; findings consistent with the documented clinical
trajectory.
Condition & Functional Status at Transfer
Awake with fluctuating attention; follows one-step commands with left arm; dense right hemiplegia; tracheostomy on trach collar; PEG for
nutrition; VP shunt in place. Ambulating short distances with maximum assistance and hemi-walker.

Follow-Up & Recommendations
1. Continue acute inpatient rehabilitation with intensive PT/OT/ST.
2. Neurology follow-up in 4 weeks; annual imaging.
3. Neurosurgery follow-up in 4 weeks for VP shunt evaluation.

5. Primary care follow-up for hypertension and diabetes management.
6. Tracheostomy care and decannulation planning at rehab.
7. Return precautions: fever, worsening neuro exam, headache, seizure activity, shunt failure signs (headache, vomiting, altered mental
status), respiratory distress, tracheostomy or PEG problems.

Procedure Detail
Under general anesthesia, right frontal ventricular catheter placed. Programmable valve tunneled subcutaneously to peritoneal cavity via

You are a senior clinical claims auditor deciding a determination for one
billed claim line. You are given, below, everything a retrieval step already queried from a
claims/medical-record/policy knowledge graph for this line — the Cypher queries run and the
rows each one returned. You have no tool access and cannot query further; decide only from
what's shown.

Domain knowledge for this review type:

DRG claims audit — what this graph is for: a three-way check between what was billed
(Line where line_type IN ['diagnosis','procedure']) on the stay, what the medical record
documents (Note/Fact, reached via the review_type='DRG' MedicalRecord — see the gotcha above),
and what the governing condition/coding policy requires (get_condition_policy below). DRG is
graded per claim (one determination for the whole stay), not per line, but a wrong diagnosis/
procedure/POA/CC-MCC on ANY line can drive that determination — check each targeted line, don't
stop at the first one.

Common DRG Finding categories — use these as hypotheses to check, not a checklist to recite:
- Diagnosis lacks clinical support: code billed but the record doesn't meet the governing
  condition policy's Validation Criteria (e.g. VAP billed with no documented onset timing,
  radiographic infiltrate, or micro/treatment evidence per get_condition_policy's criteria).
  Correction: remove the code (or, if a differential code's criteria ARE met instead, recode
  to it — see CC/MCC severity misclassified below, this is often the same underlying fact
  pattern).
- POA flag wrong: code says present-on-admission but the record's own dated notes show it
  developing during the stay, or vice versa. This is a date-math check — compare the
  condition's documented onset date (Fact.printed_date / Note.note_date) against
  Claim.claim_admit_date — not a keyword search.
- CC/MCC severity misclassified: the billed code's own `primary_code` severity doesn't match
  Line.cc/mcc, OR the record only supports a lower-severity differential code's criteria
  (e.g. J18.9 [CC] documented, not the [MCC] J95.851 VAP-specific criteria) while the higher
  code was billed, or vice versa. Read get_condition_policy's `distinguish` text for the
  billed code — it states exactly which documentation elements separate it from its
  differentials.
- Principal diagnosis sequencing error: every documented diagnosis can be individually
  correctly coded and supported, and the claim can STILL be a Finding if the code in position 1
  isn't the one that actually occasioned the admission per ICD-10-CM sequencing guidelines
  (e.g. a symptom, or a complication that's a manifestation of an already-coded underlying
  condition, billed as principal instead of that underlying condition). Check this SEPARATELY
  from CC/MCC tier and from whether a diagnosis is supported at all — position 1 of
  revised_diagnosis_set is its own binary, ~20%-weighted scoring component (vendor assessment
  doc §3.1.e), distinct from the "Remaining Codes" presence-match component.
- Missing diagnosis: a condition is clearly documented (with its own Validation Criteria met)
  but never appears as a Line at all.
- Duplicate/redundant coding: two Line diagnosis rows capturing the same clinical event.
- Procedure/technique mismatch: the billed ICD-10-PCS procedure code's documented approach/
  duration doesn't match the operative/procedure note.
- Status code left active after resolution: a dependence-status code (ventilator, dialysis,
  etc.) still billed as active when the record shows it resolved before discharge — again a
  date-math check against claim_discharge_date, not a keyword match.
- Missing procedure code: a performed procedure (e.g. "Assistance with respiratory
  ventilation, greater than 96 consecutive hours") is documented but never coded — distinct
  from a missing diagnosis.

Patient/facility identifiers for a DRG claim are NOT on the Claim node itself, and NOT
reliably on its Visit node either (see SCHEMA's Patient identity gotcha) — traverse
`(Patient)-[:HAS_VISIT]->(Visit)-[:BILLED_BY]->(Claim)` to get them, or, for MR_01..MR_10 only,
look them up on the paired readmission claim.

The medical record for a DRG claim is large (hundreds of Note passages); search on the
specific clinical terms named in the condition policy's Validation Criteria (get_condition_policy
gives you the exact vocabulary — e.g. "endotracheal", "purulent", "PaO2/FiO2") rather than a

The ICH policy requires neuroimaging confirmation of intraparenchymal blood (non-contrast CT) to validate I61 codes: - Non-contrast CT of the brain demonstrating hyperdense (acute) intraparenchymal blood collection within the brain tissue, with the radiologist's report specifying anatomic location (e.g., right basal ganglia, left thalamus, right cerebellar hemisphere) (RULE-Policy-Documents-DRG-Non-Traumatic-Intracerebral-Hemorrhage.docx-b31). These two passages together meet the policy's Validation Criteria for nontraumatic ICH and support I61.9 as the principal diagnosis. Support for obstructive hydrocephalus (keep, change severity to MCC): The H&P and neurosurgery consult document obstructive hydrocephalus with ventricular blood and recommend emergent CSF diversion: the chart documents emergent EVD placement (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n9, p.275: 3 | Emergency external ventricular drain placement) and neurosurgery recommended emergent EVD placement with drain settings (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n12, p.45: Recommendations Emergent EVD placement in the right Kocher's point; drain to 15 cmH2O above the tragus; ICP monitoring; osmotherapy; strict SBP control; follow-up CT in 6 hours). The obstructive-hydrocephalus policy designates G91.1 as MCC when imaging/provider documentation confirms obstruction (RULE-Policy-Documents-DRG-Obstructive-Hydrocephalus.docx-b8). Therefore G91.1 is supported and should carry MCC severity (policy source: RULE-Policy-Documents-DRG-Obstructive-Hydrocephalus.docx-b8). Support for acute respiratory failure with hypoxia (keep, POA=Y, MCC): Critical Care documentation demonstrates objective hypoxemia and mechanical ventilation: ABG (02:00): pH 7.32 / PaCO2 47 / PaO2 67 / HCO3 20; P/F 70 (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n11, p.721). The acute-respiratory-failure policy allows presumption of objective hypoxemia when the provider documents initiation of invasive mechanical ventilation for respiratory failure (RULE-Policy-Documents-DRG-Acute-Respiratory-Failure-with-Hypoxia.docx-b37). The H&P and progress notes document emergent intubation for airway protection on presentation (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n9, p.275: Rapid-sequence intubation was performed for airway protection) and an active problem of prolonged mechanical ventilation (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n9, p.275: 5 | Acute respiratory failure with prolonged mechanical ventilation). These meet the policy criteria for J96.01. Support for ventilator-associated Klebsiella pneumonia (J15.9 and B96.1, POA=N): Medication Administration records show treatment with cefepime specifically for Klebsiella VAP (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1251, p.694: Cefepime | 2 g | IV q8h | 08/01-08/08 | Klebsiella VAP) and the discharge summary documents a hospital-acquired Klebsiella ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with cefepime (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1262, p.1052: hospital-acquired Klebsiella pneumoniae ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with cefepime). POA=N for VAP is correct. Procedures supported (kept): EVD insertion and VP shunt are documented. VP shunt operative note documents right frontal ventriculostomy to peritoneum and distal catheter placement (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n122, p.43: Under general anesthesia, right frontal ventricular catheter placed. Programmable valve tunneled subcutaneously to peritoneal cavity via mini-laparotomy.). Arterial-line placement is documented (Procedure Note - Arterial Line - Right Radial supports arterial monitoring; conflict checking favors the right radial arterial line procedure note; NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n18, p.97: Indication for Procedure: Tight blood pressure monitoring for SBP < 140). Tracheostomy and PEG placement are documented throughout the chart and discharge (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1251, p.127 and NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1262, p.1052). Ventilation >96 hours is supported by the active problem list and the prolonged course requiring tracheostomy (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n9, p.275: 5 | Acute respiratory failure with prolonged mechanical ventilation). ETT insertion is supported by the ED/H&P and progress notes (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n9, p.275: Rapid-sequence intubation was performed for airway protection). Unsupported / removed diagnoses and rationale: - I97.5 (Nontraumatic subdural hemorrhage) - removed. Imaging/interpretation and neurology/neurosurgery documentation consistently describe a left basal-ganglia intraparenchymal (hypertensive) hemorrhage with intraventricular extension; the MRI/radiology and consult notes do not document a subdural hematoma (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n42, p.276: Large left basal-ganglia hematoma with expected evolution pattern. No underlying vascular malformation identified. IVH resolving.). The ICH policy explicitly distinguishes intraparenchymal ICH from extraparenchymal subdural hemorrhage (RULE-Policy-Documents-DRG-Non-Traumatic-Intracerebral-Hemorrhage.docx-b11). There is no radiology/provider documentation supporting a subdural diagnosis, so I97.5 should be removed. - A39.0 (Meningococcal meningitis) - removed. No clinical, laboratory, imaging, or infectious-disease documentation of meningitis or meningococcal infection was found; the infectious complication documented and treated was Klebsiella VAP (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1251, p.694; NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1262, p.1052). Without supporting documentation, A39.0 is not supported. - E22.2 (SIADH) - removed. The chart documents cerebral salt wasting with targeted therapy (fludrocortisone) rather than SIADH: Fludrocortisone | 0.1 mg | PO/PEG BID | 08/08-08/13 | Cerebral salt wasting (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1251, p.127). The documentation supports cerebral salt wasting (a different entity) and does not support SIADH coding. - Z98.62 (Presence of intracranial neurostimulator) - removed. The record documents a VP shunt and EVD but no intracranial neurostimulator device; discharge/transfer and procedure notes list VP shunt and tracheostomy/PEG without mention of a neurostimulator or its implantation (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1258, p.168: Your brain shunt (VP shunt) drains fluid from your brain to your abdomen; watch for signs of shunt malfunction ...). Absent documentation specific to a neurostimulator, Z98.62 is unsupported. POA / severity corrections: - G91.1 (Obstructive hydrocephalus): billed as CC but policy designates obstructive hydrocephalus as MCC when criteria are met (RULE-Policy-Documents-DRG-Obstructive-Hydrocephalus.docx-b8). The documentation meets obstructive-hydrocephalus criteria (ventricular blood and EVD/VP shunt management), so set severity to MCC. - G81.94 (Hemiplegia, right dominant) and R47.1 (dysarthria): both are clearly present on presentation (H&P documents dense right hemiplegia and inability to speak on arrival). POA should be Y (present on admission) rather than N as billed (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n9, p.275: dense right hemiplegia; "... he couldn't move his right side or speak." and the admission neuro exam). Update POA accordingly. - Z99.11 (Dependence on respirator status): documentation shows emergent intubation on presentation and prolonged ventilator dependence with subsequent tracheostomy; POA should be Y (present at/very near admission) rather than billed N (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n9, p.275: Rapid-sequence intubation was performed for airway protection; NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1262, p.1052: tracheostomy-dependent respiratory status). Procedures removed for lack of specific documentation in the retrieved chart: - 02HV33Z (Insertion of infusion device into superior vena cava, percutaneous approach) - removed. The record documents multiple central infusions and lines were used, but there is no specific procedural note or operative report found in the retrieved chart that documents insertion of an infusion device into the SVC (the discharge/procedure summaries list EVD, VP shunt, tracheostomy, PEG, arterial line but not a tunneled/implanted infusion device into the SVC) (NOTE-Medical-Records-16-30-MR_19.pdf-n1262, p.1052). Keep all other billed procedures that have specific procedure or problem-list documentation (ETT insertion, EVD, VP shunt, arterial line, tracheostomy, PEG, prolonged ventilation assistance >96 hrs). result.rationale_letter: To: Medical Records / Coding Department Re: Audit of Inpatient Claim MR_19 - Determination and Required Coding Corrections We performed a DRG-focused audit of the entire inpatient encounter for patient MR_19. We compared the billed diagnosis and procedure list against the medical record and the applicable coding validation policies. Below is our determination and the corrective action required. Finding: The medical record supports the principal diagnosis of nontraumatic intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH) with intraventricular extension and obstructive hydrocephalus, together with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring prolonged mechanical ventilation and a ventilator-associated Klebsiella pneumonia. However, several billed diagnosis and one billed procedure lack clinical documentation meeting policy validation criteria and must be removed from the coded claim. Basis (examples of supporting documentation relied on): - The admission H&P documents emergent CT demonstrating a large left basal-ganglia intracerebral hemorrhage with intraventricular extension and obstructive hydrocephalus (Clinical note: Priya Ranganathan, MD; 07/23/2026) - this satisfies the ICH imaging/provider documentation requirement for an I61.- code. - Neurosurgery documented emergent EVD placement for obstructive hydrocephalus and later performed a ventriculoperitoneal shunt when hydrocephalus persisted (operative note 08/09/2026). These procedures meet the surgical validation pathway for ICH and hydrocephalus coding. - Critical care ABG documented PaO2 67 mm Hg and a P/F ratio of 70, and the chart documents emergent intubation and prolonged mechanical ventilation with subsequent tracheostomy; these facts satisfy the acute hypoxemic respiratory failure criteria for J96.01 (policy presumption for objective hypoxemia with provider-documented invasive ventilation). - The chart documents Klebsiella ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with cefepime during the admission (medication administration and discharge summary). Corrections required (summary): - Remove diagnoses not supported by the medical record: I97.5 (nontraumatic subdural hemorrhage), A39.0 (meningococcal meningitis), E22.2 (SIADH), and Z98.62 (intracranial neurostimulator) - these conditions are not documented in the radiology/operative/consultation notes or are contradicted by documented alternative diagnoses (e.g., cerebral salt wasting documented and treated rather than SIADH; intraparenchymal basal ganglia hemorrhage documented rather than subdural hematoma). - Correct severity/POA where chart evidence requires it: G91.1 obstructive hydrocephalus meets MCC criteria per policy and documentation (change severity to MCC); G81.94 (hemiplegia, right) and R47.1 (dysarthria) are documented on presentation and should be POA=Y; Z99.11 (dependence on respirator) is present at/near admission and should be POA=Y. - Remove procedure 02HV33Z (insertion of infusion device into SVC) - no procedural note or operative report in the record documents this specific procedure, whereas EVD, VP shunt, arterial line, tracheostomy, PEG, and prolonged ventilation ARE documented. Corrected coding outcome: the claim should retain I61.9 as principal diagnosis and keep the supported high-severity comorbidities and procedures (see the attached revised diagnosis and procedure lists). Please update the coded claim accordingly and re-submit. If you disagree with removal of any code above, please provide the specific source documentation that supports the removed code (operative note, radiology report, or treating-provider note with date/time) so we can reconsider. Absent such documentation, the removals above stand. Sincerely, Senior Clinical Claims Auditor

code_decisions.reason: Imaging and provider documentation (admission H&P and radiology) confirm a left basal-ganglia intraparenchymal hemorrhage with IVH and obstructive hydrocephalus, meeting the policy's ICH validation criteria.
No radiology or consult documentation supports a subdural hemorrhage; imaging and consults document a basal-ganglia intraparenchymal hemorrhage with IVH instead.
Chart documents refractory intracranial hypertension requiring osmotic therapy, which supports cerebral edema as an active diagnosis during this admission.
Imaging and neurosurgery documentation describe obstructive hydrocephalus due to IVH with emergent CSF diversion; policy designates obstructive hydrocephalus as MCC when criteria are met.
GCS 6 on arrival and ongoing decreased consciousness are documented in the admission and progress notes, supporting a coma diagnosis.
Objective hypoxemia (PaO2 67, P/F 70) and provider-documented invasive ventilation for respiratory failure meet the policy criteria for acute hypoxemic respiratory failure.
Medication administration and discharge summary document hospital-acquired ventilator-associated Klebsiella pneumonia treated during the admission; POA=N is correct.
Microorganism (Klebsiella) is documented as the cause of the VAP and treated accordingly; POA=N is consistent with hospital-acquired infection.
The chart documents cerebral salt wasting (treated with fludrocortisone) rather than SIADH; there is no documentation supporting SIADH, so E22.2 is unsupported.
Past medical history documents essential hypertension present on admission.
Past medical history documents type 2 diabetes present on admission.
Past medical history documents hyperlipidemia present on admission.
Dense right hemiplegia is documented on initial exam and progress notes; POA should be Y. Billed laterality is supported; change POA to reflect presence on arrival.
Admission H&P documents inability to speak on presentation; dysarthria/aphasia is present on admission.
The record documents a VP shunt and EVD but no intracranial neurostimulator operative note or device documentation; absence of any neurostimulator documentation makes Z98.62 unsupported.
Emergent intubation at presentation and later tracheostomy-dependent respiratory status at transfer are documented; dependence on ventilator/trach should be coded as present on admission/encounter.
No documentation of meningococcal meningitis was found; the infectious complication documented was Klebsiella VAP. A39.0 is unsupported.
Emergent rapid-sequence intubation for airway protection is documented on presentation.
Emergent external ventricular drain placement is documented and was the neurosurgical response to obstructive hydrocephalus.
Operative note documents ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement (right frontal ventriculostomy to peritoneum) for persistent communicating hydrocephalus.

No procedural note or operative report documenting insertion of an infusion device into the SVC was found in the retrieved chart; discharge and procedure summaries list other devices (EVD, VP shunt, tracheostomy, PEG, arterial line) but not an infusion device into the SVC.
Arterial-line placement for tight blood-pressure monitoring is documented (procedure note/nursing assessment), supporting insertion of a monitoring device into an upper artery.
Percutaneous tracheostomy is documented as performed for prolonged ventilator dependence; discharge also documents tracheostomy-dependent respiratory status.
PEG placement is listed in the active problem list and the discharge/transfer instructions document ongoing tube feedings and PEG care.
Chart documents prolonged mechanical ventilation requiring tracheostomy and ongoing ventilator dependence; the active problem list explicitly lists prolonged mechanical ventilation.

Payer policy and coding guideline passages on G81 codes:
[DOC-Policy-Documents-DRG-Ischemic-Stroke-and-Post-Stroke-Neurological-Deficits.docx › Definitions › Post-Stroke Neurological Deficit Codes]
ICD-10-CM requires specificity for hemiplegia laterality (G81.91 = right dominant, G81.92 = right non-dominant, G81.93 = left dominant, G81.94 = left non-dominant) based on the patient's handedness and affected side. Providers often document 'right-sided weakness' or 'left hemiplegia' without specifying dominance. Per ICD-10-CM guidelines (Section I.C.9.d), when dominance is not documented, the affected side is assumed to be the dominant side when the dominant side is affected, or the default code for unspecified side (G81.90) may be used. Auditors should query for dominant/non-dominant status when the affected side and handedness are not both documented.

[DOC-Policy-Documents-DRG-Ischemic-Stroke-and-Post-Stroke-Neurological-Deficits.docx › Definitions › Post-Stroke Neurological Deficit Codes]
Per ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines Section I.C.9.d, when a patient has a current cerebral infarction (I63.-) with associated neurological deficits, additional codes from categories G81 (hemiplegia and hemiparesis), G82 (paraplegia and tetraplegia), G83 (other paralytic syndromes), R47.1 (dysarthria), G81.9x (hemiplegia, unspecified side), or other applicable deficit codes are assigned to capture the specific neurological deficit. These codes carry their own CC/MCC weight and are critical for accurate DRG assignment. The ICD-10-CM guidelines also address coding of late effects of stroke (I69.-) for deficits present after the acute stroke encounter is concluded. Laterality codes for hemiplegia must specify dominant vs. non-dominant side when documented.

[DOC-Policy-Documents-DRG-Ischemic-Stroke-and-Post-Stroke-Neurological-Deficits.docx › Coding Considerations › Physician Query Scenario]
A 74-year-old right-hand-dominant male is admitted with acute left-sided hemiplegia and expressive aphasia of 3-hour duration. MRI DWI demonstrates a right MCA territory infarction. CTA head shows M1 segment MCA occlusion. The patient receives IV tPA followed by mechanical thrombectomy with mTICI 2b reperfusion. At discharge on day 5, the neurology note documents 'residual mild left arm weakness and expressive aphasia, improving.' The discharge summary lists 'right MCA ischemic stroke.'
